I am advised that the larger part of this $300,000 will be paid on account of the bridge.
The hon. minister surely has the details showing what he wants this $300,000 for V
This is largely to pay the bridge contractor.
Wlmt is the amount ?
The total estimate for the year 1903, for each of these branches of service was : The bridge, $029.533 ; construction of branch, $308,634 ; rolling stock, $12,245.
What was the amount available for each of these services ?
These figures were estimated to cover all the expenses from the 30th September, 1902, to the end of 1903. I did not catch the hon. gentleman's last question.
What was the amount voted for each of these items ?
The vote was general. It was not divided. It was $500,000 in the main estimates, lint it was not divided in the way I have described.

The hon. minister is not dealing with a prospective work, but, with work that has been done, and we ought to have before we pass an item of this kind, some particulars that will justify us in voting this money. Last year I called attention to this very point. In the preceding year the then hon. Minister of Railways and Canals had entered into a contract with certain contractors to complete the first section of this line. On the completion of that first section, without asking for tenders, without getting a report from his engineers, without any consideration whatever apparently of what the nature of the work on the second section was, the government accepted an offer of the contractors to do the work on the second section on the same terms as they had done the first. I pointed out then how absurd such a thing was, because the work on the second section might be worth double or only one-half of what it was per mile on the first section and yet the government had entered into that contract and had then asked parliament to vote the money without the slightest knowledge of what they were doing and they did that, not only in defiance of every business principle, but in the very teeth of the provision of the

statute which prevents them from doing anything of the kind. Now, we see the result. The then lion. Minister of Railways and Canals asked from parliament a grant of a sum of money to carry out what he then proposed. We find now that so indefinite or uncertain were the materials upon which he was acting, that the government came down with a proposition asking us for $450,000 more than they asked a year ago, and the hon. Minister of Finance now says that he is willing to take one-third from the amount and reduce the $450,000 to $300,000. Surely under these circumstances we are entitled to ask the hon. minister to tell us precisely what this bridge was going to cost last year and what the miles of road to be built were to cost. In each of these items the vote has been found wanting. We are not now talking of the future ; we are talking about the past. This money is to be expended for work done during the past year. The officers of the department know how much the then hon. Minister of Railways and Canals asked last year for the bridge and how much for the miles of railway to be built. Would the hon. minister tell us how much more the bridge has cost than was anticipated, and how much more the railway cost than was anticipated ?

I am sorry I do not deserve to be complimented on reducing this item by $150,000, if it conveys the impression that we are reducing the cost of the work. It simply means that we have only been able to do $300,000 worth of work up to the 30th June, but the remaining $150,000 will have to be provided for in the estimates of the coming year. Perhaps my hon. friend did not understand that.
Mr. BA RKEIi.	I understand that, and I
also understand that I cannot see how a business department, a railway department, some weeks ago would say that they require $450,000 to pay for work done up to the 30th of June, and now find out that they only require $300,000.
These estimates were prepared by the department, not some weeks ago, but several months ago.
The supplementary estimates ?

It is only fair to the railway officials to state that the explanations on which these items are based were prepared some considerable time ago. It is a large sum of money, and it is my duty to furnish all information that the committee may desire. I am quite content to let the item stand and I wish that hon. gentlemen would specify the points on which they desire information.

We are entitled to have the fullest particulars that would be required by any company from an officer who
asks for $300,000 or $450,000 more than he expected to ask for a certain work. If the hon. gentleman can tell us to-night how much was expected to be expended on i)he construction of the road and how much upon this bridge, perhaps we will be satisfied.

There is no difference in the estimate, but only a difference in the volume of work that was done under contract during a certain time. It is ill}' duty to give the hon. gentleman a full answer and I will do so, but I would not have him think that there was any mistake in the estimates.

Does the minister wish the House to understand that a year ago we were asked to authorize the expenditure of a certain amount on account of a bridge or on account of ten miles of railway, and not that we were asked to authorize what would be expended during the year?
The whole amount of the contract will be given to my hon. friend and whether the work is done last year or this year_or next year the amount must be paid. This is a large and very expensive work.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) makes no mistake when he says that the estimate for a particular year is exceeded, and we want to know why it was exceeded and in what particular ? This is a lump sum for the Hillsborough branch and the bridge, but they are two distinct contracts, and they must be separated'.
When the matter comes up again I will be very glad to give to the hon. gentleman a statement showing the expenditure on the bridge and on the road. Let the item stand.

It would be very satisfactory to the committee to have the certificates of the government engineers upon which payments have been made during the year. I think this is the same contractor as for the Quebec bridge.

No. This contractor is Mr. Haney. The certificates of the engineers will be as to the amount of work done at each time payment is claimed. I will bring a statement of the amount that has been paid during the year on each of the contracts, and it follows that these sums have only been paid upon the certificate of the engineers.
It would be satisfactory to know the estimate of the work to be done between now and the time this $300,000 is expended.
This is for past work. It is due but not paid.
When will the Murray Harbour branch be completed?

The
deputy informs me that the time for the [DOT]completion of the contract will expire next fall.
Does that refer to the bridge ?
It refers to the substructure.
When will the bridge be completed ?

The
steel bridge which is now used over one of the large rivers on the main line is to be moved over to Prince Edward Island. The arrangements have not yet been made for that.
It is an old steel bridge.
It is a good steel bridge, but it is not adapted to its present traffic.
When is it expected that the entire bridge will be completed ?
It is [DOT]expected that the substructure will be completed during the fall, and that in the spring the bridge will be placed in position and the whole work completed next season.
Why are you buying rolling stock now if the work is not to be completed until next year ?
Two locomotives are being built at Kingston. They are not yet completed. They have been ordered for future delivery. They will be ready next December. [DOT]
Might I ask the Minister of Finance from what part of the Intercolonial does this old bridge come ?
With regard to the rolling stock, a few cars have been built for use in the course of construction. These are built in the shops at "Charlottetown.
They have been built, I suppose, for the use of the contractors, because no one else can use them ?
Yes ; some of them are hired to the contractors.
With regard to the bridge, I understand that the substructure only is the work of contractors, and the superstructure is the work of the government ?

Yes ; the work of the government, by moving a bridge from the mainland.
Mr. HACKETT, What will the substructure cost ?

The estimate of the total cost of tine bridge is Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
$1,494,000 ; but I have not the difference between the cost of the superstructure and the cost of the substructure. That I will get for my hon. friend when the matter comes up again.

I understand that the government of Prince Edward Island are bound to pay a certain amount in connection with this bridge. Are the approaches kept up by the government of Frince Edward Island or the government of Canada ?
There is a contract between the Dominion government and the island government on the subject. I shall be glad to bring it down, but I would not care to speak of its terms tonight.

You have bound down the government of Prince Edward Island to $10,000 a year in connection with this bridge. How are the driveways arranged ? Can the ordinary farmer drive his carriage on the bridge while trains are moving over it ?

The minister, of course, held negotiations with the representatives of the island government on that subject, and I shall be glad to bring down a copy of the contract. I am afraid I could not tell my hon. friend very much about the arrangements other than those in the contract. It will have to speak for itself.
Are the approaches to the bridge to be maintained by the Dominion government or by the provincial government ?
The deputy minister informs me that he is not very clear on that point, and I would rather not give a definite answer.

Another matter in connection with the island railway which I would like to refer to is the necessity of building a branch line of railway from O'Leary's station to the west shore of the island. I asked a question about this some weeks ago, and the minister told me that it was under consideration. Has the minister decided on that matter yet ?
No decision has been come to in the matter since the minister last answered the hon. gentleman's question.
Is it still under consideration ?
I think so.

Would the hon. gentleman, if possible, have a survey made of that locality during the present year ? We do not want an expenditure of public money that will not be of some service. My hon. friend here says it is an election dodge.

There is no election dodge about it. There is no part of the province that is more in want of railway accommodation than that section. I insist on the minister having a survey at least made this year.
I am afraid that I must not definitely promise my hon. friend a survey. I can only say that the matter will come under consideration.

If the hon. minister will bring down a full statement of the cost of the bridge, the estimated cost of the branch and the arrangements with the Prince Edward Island government for the approaches-if he will bring down the full text of the agreement, and give the House all the information in one body, the members will be able to grasp the situation much better than they could by getting the information piecemeal.
I will do so.	[DOT]
At the same time a statement of the rolling stock that was paid for last year, and the amount the government are receiving from the contractors for the use of it.
The hon. minister said that he was purchasing some engines from the Kingston Locomotive Works. Did they secure the contract after public competition ?
Yes, there were tenders.
What other companies tendered at the same time, and what was the difference in the prices asked ?
I think there are only two works in Canada engaged in the locomotive business. They were both asked to tender.
Will the hon. minister bring down the prices ?
Yes.
Are ail the engines on the Intercolonial Railway procured from the Canadian locomotive shops, or are some procured from the American shops ?

We are now discussing the Prince Edward Island Railway, which is not a part of the Intercolonial, but my hon. friend's question is quite in order. We have had some American engines, but the great difficulty has been to get engines anywhere.
Mr.. CLARICE. Will the hon. gentleman bring down a memo, showing the cost of all the engines purchased ?
Is not the Prince Edward Island Railway a part of the Intercolonial Railway ?
It is part of the Canadian government railway system, but not of the Intercolonial Railway. The acounts are separate.
Was not a petition sent in for a further extension of this line from Belfast to Murray Harbour ?
There lias been an application for an extension of the road, about five miles, which is under consideration.

In my opinion there is need Of extensions in the other parts of the island. My hon. friend from West Prince called attention to the necessity of an extension to the western part of the island, where the people are as energetic and prosperous as in the eastern part. These people desire railway accommodation and I see no reason why their request should not be granted. Largely signed petitions have been presented during the last three or four sessions for such extensions, and I believe that the project was considered in 1890 and an Order in Council passed for the building of branch lines. The one I particularly refer to is between Crapaud and North Wiltshire. It would go through a very populous section where there is no railway accommodation. In some places the people are upwards of twenty ntiles away from the main line. I should think that if railway accommodation is to be given to other sections, these places should be considered.

With regard to this work between O'Leary station and the west shore of the island, I would again call attention to its importance. The people in that section desire facilities for the marketing of their products in the fall of the year. At present they are obliged to cart their produce some twelve or fifteen miles to the railway, which causes them great loss. While we are voting away millions of money in other sections of the country, there is no reason why Prince Edward Island should not receive its share. I remember not many years ago, when the hon. Minister of Finance was visiting the Island with the object of securing the election of a supporter of the government, he held out to the people at several meetings, not only in the principal towns and villages, but also in the country school houses, that the government were going to do everything possible for the island. By his personal magnetism and large promises lie succeeded in getting his candidate elected. We now ask him to pay some attention to our province. It is not only the town of Summerside and the city of Charlottetown that deserves consideration, but the country districts as well. The man who works on his farm from early morning to late at night, endeavouring to maintain his family, is deserving of consideration. I had the pleasure and honour of attending n num-

her of those meetings which the hon. gentleman addressed. There was one especially ill the village of Emerald, which the people attended in large numbers. At that meeting a former member of this parliament, the Hon. Peter Sinclair presided, and one of the inducements held out to the electors was that a branch line would be built from North Wiltshire to Crapaud. That was one of the great inducements held out by the hon. minister. yet nothing has been done since.
The hon. gentleman is well aware how things are in the island. He knows that the branch from O'Leary station to Cape Wolfe should be built aud also the other branch from North Wiltshire to Crapaud. I may say that the hon. gentleman who represents East Queen's (Mr. MacKinnon) is also interested in the matter, and have no doubt we will hear from him on this occasion.

I cannot think that my hon. friend from West Prince is very serious when he talks of any promises which I held out to the people. I assure him he is entirely mistaken. I do not remember the particular meeting to which he refers, but I remember a series of pleasant meetings which we had in the island, but at which I am sure I held out no hopes of anything. When he says that I assured the people that tire government had done its utmost for Prince Edward Island and would always continue to do so, I plead guilty to that soft impeachment, but I never made a promise to construct a branch to North Wiltshire or anywhere else. I do not blame my hon. friend for pressing on the government those railway improvements, but I would not like him to base his argument on the assumption that I ever premised anything.
I wish to say a few words on this vote.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Let me put the motion to reduce the vote. This is not closing the discussion on the item. I am merely putting the vote for reduction.
Mr. LEFUR6EY. The hon. gentleman's (Mr. MacKinnon) new constituency extends through Crapaud and North Wiltshire, and no doubt he wants to advocate a branch line. It would not be fair to cut him off.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is no attempt to cut the hon. gentleman off.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. MacKinnon) was on his feet when you put the question, Mr. Chairman. It may be that he does not want the item reduced. He may want this odd $150,000 left to be used for the extension he wishes to advocate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am not trying to cut the hon. gentleman (Mr. MacKinnon) off. There was an amendment to reduce the item from $450,000 to $300,000. I take it that nobody objects to the reduc-Mr. HACKETT.
tion. I put that amendment, and when it is carried the item as amended, a vote of $300,000 is still open for discussion.

I have no objection to reduce the amount. But I desire to make a few remarks upon the merits of the question. I am somewhat surprised that hon. gentlemen should oppose the passing of this amendment. The supplementary estimates have been before the House for a considerable time. They were prepared by officials of the department some months ago, and they show that $300,000 is necessary. There is no need of members of the opposition objecting to the amount, because the officials are men of experience, and they -would see to it that the amounts paid up to-the end of June last are properly expended, and certificates properly given before any expenditure is made.
The amount has been expended.

Yes, expended up to-the end of June last. But I would ask why this hesitancy on the part of members of the opposition to vote this money. For it should be known that the building of these extensions is the main plank in the platform of the Liberal-Conservative party in Prince Edward Island. Let me read just one resolution from the proceedings of the conference of Liberal-Conservatives held in-Charlottetown on January last :
-Moved by E. Hackett, M.P., seconded by R. McNeill, M.D., -and carried unanimously.
Whereas the policy ot the Liberal-Conservative party is to construct branch lines ot railway in this province ;
Therefore, resolved, that this conference desires to place itself on record as supporting the building ot branch lines proposed by the Liberal-Conservatives at the session of 1896.
Now, hon. gentlemen in this House will remember that the Liberal-Conservatives, then in power, proposed to build some seven or eight roads in Prince Edward Island, and there is need for a number of branch roads there, and it is for the purpose of pointing that out that I rose. I would like hon. members of the opposition to co-operate with the hon. member for East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey). and the hon. member for West Prince (Mr. Hackett) and show their good will toward Prince Edward Island in tills matter. Since confederation Prince Edward Island lias not been treated fairly up to a few years ago in tlie expenditure of public money, I speak in a business way. Prince Edward Island is entitled to all the necessary railway accommodations that can be provided by parliament. It is necessary to have a railway to West Cape and also to Crapaud, a thriving village, and Montague and other sections as well as to Murray Harbour South. I would like to show the position of this matter in a few figures if hon. members will extend their patience. According to the last report of the Minister of Railways, in the whole of Canada

prior to and since confederation, the amount expended upon railways on capital account, up to June 30th, 1902, is $136,990,338.42. If you add the subsidies to railways in the different provinces other than Prince Edward Island you find the total expenditure on railways was $258,860,655.11. In addition, there is the government expenditure on the canals, amounting to $83,519,103.86 on capital account. If you include the amount spent on consolidated fund, you have a total expenditure on canals of $102,484,545.76. This makes a total expenditure of $361,345,200 on railways and canals. There is miscellaneous expenditure on both of these of $557,034.27, or a total expenditure on railways and canals up to June 30th, 1902, of $361,902,835.14. The total expenditure on railways in Prince Edward Island is $4,599,825.15. There has been no expenditure on canals-we have not yet realized that a canal is necessary. Prior to confederation the colonial government of Prince Edward Island expended on railways $3,144,735.11 of the sum over four millions I mentioned. From confederation down to the present time, there has been a little pittance of a few hundred thousand dollars to build thirteen miles of railway to Cape Traverse. That is all that had been done for the province when we began building to Belfast and Murray harbour through a large section that greatly needed a railway. The people have been settled there for a hundred years or more. The place is thickly settled-Prince Edward Island, I believe, is the most thickly settled portion of the Dominion. And to-day the people are going into a different kind of farming. As was pointed out by the hon. member for West Prince (Mr. Hackett) they are going into more intense cultivation of the soil, market gardening, dairying, stock-raising, and so on. and their products must be sent to market quickly. This is the great object in having a railway there. Now, not for the purpose of finding fault, but for the sake of argument, I wish to refer to another ease. I find that the amount paid by the D minion government for railways in Cape Breton is $3,860,679.14. This was all spent, by the Dominion, for Cape Breton was a part of Nova Scotia before .confederation and had not a colonial government of its own. This large expenditure on railways has taken place in Cape Breton, yet there is hesitancy on the part of hon. members to favour the construction of this branch railway in Prince Edward Island and a bridge across the Hillsborough river, although Prince Edward Island had compared more than creditably with the rest of Canada in railway construction in colonial days. The railway extension amounted to only about ten million dollars elsewhere in Canada before confederation. I may say about the railway, that it has never paid better in its history, the revenues last year is the greatest on record. The management of
the road is also better. I may add that the bridge is being constructed jointly. The province is contributing about $10,000 a year, and the Dominion government is constructing the bridge. It is to be used for passengers and carriages as well as for ears. I hope the House will mt hesitate to make this grant. Prince Edward Island is not getting too much. Some hon. members speak as If Prince Edward Island is getting too much. I am ready to sit down with any business man and prove to him that' it is getting a fair expenditure in the light of the little expenditure of the past. We are going to ask for a railway that my hon. friend from West Prince (Mr. Hackett) wants, and others, and I think we should have more railway extension to develop our country. The people are thrifty and well merit modern means of travel and trade.

The argument used by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Mackinnon) is oue of the most extraordinary I ever heard in this House. The hon. gentleman contends that Prince Edward Island must have money spent in it. It is not with him a question of whether the public works are necessary, but how much money is to be spent there, quite regardless of the need of public works. Now, I hope there is not an hon. gentleman on either side of this House who objects to necessary public works in any of the provinces. Nobody objects to a public work being built in Prince Edward Island when it is required. What we object to is building public works in Prince Edward Island at a cost greater than they ought to cost. That is the whole case, and yet the hon. gentleman ignores it entirely. The hon. gentleman forgets that we find on this paper that the officials to whom he appeals asked for $450,000 for a work for which they are now willing to accept $300,000. Is that not a complete justification of the inquiry we are making ? After we begin this discussion, after $450,000 has been put on these estimates and has remained there for weeks, then we find that $300,000 is all that is needed. The hon. gentleman, according to his argument, would say that we ought to have allowed the $450,000 to pass without a word. We find here an estimate from the government asking $450,000 for this work,, and as soon as the discussion commences and we ask questions about it, the minister tells us they only want something like seventy per cent of the sum, and the hou. gentleman is absolutely horrified that members on this side should question anything that appears in these estimates. What we have very properly pointed out is that this work is the one that, last vear. w^e were asked to grant money for ; the money was asked by the responsible minister without j the ordinary care of a business man. No i tender was asked for. though the statute

requires the minister to ask for tenders and require him to let the work in a particular way. That statute was absolutely ignored, and we are asked now, twelve months afterwards, to. pass an estimate to cover up the shortage of the hon. gentleman.

I do not think any objection can be taken to any of the hon. member's inquiries, 1 admit that all he lias asked for in the way of information is proper. But I do emphatically object to his assumption that the reduction of this sum from $450,000 to $300,000 has anything to do with the cost of the work. It has nothing to do with the cost of the work, it is simply a question of how much money will be expended in a given period. Several months ago, as far back as February, the departmental officials made an estimate in which they thought as much as $450,000 would be earned on the contract by the first day of .Tune. Now that the year is ended we find that only $300,000 has been earned. But the balance will have to be paid in tbe current year. Therefore, the reduction does not touch the question of expense of the undertaking at all. It does not prove there has been any mistake in estimating the cost of the work, it does not prove the estimates have been too high, it does not prove that the cost of any portion of the work is too high ; it simply proves that the quantity of work done within a given period has not been as great as the officials some months ago supposed it would be.

The hon. gentleman has overlooked the fact that I was replying to the argument of the hon. member for East Queen's (Mr. Mackinnon). That hon. gentleman was contending that it was improper and unreasonable for vis to question the figures given by tlie officers of the department. Here we have in this printed paper the figures of the officers of the department asking for $450,000, and it was after we began to question this that we find that only $300,000 is needed. Is not that a complete answer to the hon. gentleman's argument that what these responsible officials say should go ? In reply to the minister. I have already referred to how it happened that this $300,000 is required to be voted on this occasion. I pointed out last year that the whole, work upon which the vote of last year was taken and of which this Is a supplement, was absolutely illegal.

I am afraid I have to take exception to another remark of the lipn. gent leman, and* that is that it was only when they began questioning the minister that they found there was to be a reduction. The reduction of $150,000 was noted by the officials for my information, and the motion was made as soon as I had an opportunity of making it.
Will you require $150,000 to finish this work in addition to the $300,000 now voted ?
Yes.

As this is the last item on the Intercolonial, I wish to remind the minister that we will want, on the next item, a statement of the receipts and expenditures of the Intercolonial during the last current year to the 30th of June, 1903. We must have it now. We want also to know what amount of the $275,000 for steel rails and fastenings went into the road during the past year, or whether it only went into stores. We want to discuss the principle of charging for the steel rails : what amount of that is charged to capital and what to income account. The minister repeated his statement In reference to the position taken by my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker). My hon. friend does not mean that because the minister expended $300,000 over and above the estimates asked for last year, that necessarily $300,000 more will be expended on tbe bridge. He never contended anything of the kind. What he found fault with was the estimate of tbe department. It is just as bad to over-estimate the amount of the expenditure as to under-estimate it. The estimate ought t,o have been correct, and witli the information which has been brought down to-day we do not know how this money has been expended. There are two distinct and different contracts-on,e for the bridge and one for the extension of the railway. We do not know how much has been overexpended, on the bridge or on the rest of tbe work, of the amount voted last year. How did there come to be an over-expenditure in excess of the engineer's estimate ? not at all contending that this is an amount in excess of the ultimate cost of the work, but we find that we cannot get correct estimates from the department as to the expenditure. There is another point in regard to the $150,000. This estimate was compiled two months ago. as the hon. minister says, or within less than two months of tlie end of the fiscal year. Why is it that the officers of the department are $150,000 astray ? There is no apology for it. They knew up to the end of May what the expenditure was. These estimates are prepared after the end of May, and they only had to calculate what would be tbe over-expenditure for June. How is it that they are $150,000 astray 7 These estimates are prepared in lump sums, not accurate estimates such as the House of Commons ought to have from the minister at the head of the department. but just estimates taken at random as to what the expenditure may be. The minister should be able to tell us within $10,000 what the over-expenditure was during the year. That is what I complain about. However, as this is the

last item, I will ask the hon. minister to see that the information that I have asked for is furnished at least before the debate on this question comes to a close. I want the information in time to look over it for the purpose of debating some of these items. The information ought to have been furnished to the House six weeks ago. I have asked for this information preparatory to the consideration of these estimates for the purpose of discussing a subject which arose in the debate between the hon. exMinister of Railways and Canals and myself in reference to some statements that he had made. I ask that it shall be furnished promptly so that we will be able to discuss the question intelligently when it comes up. As this item is to stand I will not discuss it any further than to ask that the information in reference to the expenditure on the bridge and in reference to the expenditure on the rest of the work be given in detail, together with the amount which is required for both. I am particularly anxious to get some information in regard to the $20,000 which the hon. Minister of Finance says has been expended t6 furnish rolling stock to be hired to the contractor, which is not customary at all. We want to know what will be necessary to complete the bridge, as well as the total expenditure on the line.

I think my hon. friend is wrong in stating that I had said that $20,000 was expended on rolling stock. According to this memorandum the total expenditure on rolling stock from the 30th June, 1902, was $5,000 odd, and for the 30th June, 1903, $7,000, making about $12,000. There ai-e two classes of estimates. In regard to one of these classes of estimates, it is important that the engineer shall be reasonably accurate, because if he is not so it will affect his professional reputation, 'and that is the estimate of the probable cost of a work. I am afraid that from listening to this discussion some hon. gentlemen may have gathered the impi'ession that the officers of the department were $150,000 out in their estimate of the cost of this work. It is not so at all.
We did not say that at all.

My hon. friend may not so understand it, but many hon. gentlemen may have gathered the impression from what was said. It is assumed that the officers of the department have been iii en'or to the extent of $150,000 in their estimates. I am advised that these estimates were prepared by the officials of the Railway Department as far back as February last, which was before the beginning of the work of the season, and it would be an exceedingly difficult thing for an engineer to estimate the amount of work a contractor would do within a
given period. I simply want to make the point clear. Pei'haps the hon. member for Hamilton did not so understand it and perhaps the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Ilaggart) did not so understand it. but lest the impression get abroad from this discussion that there was an error in the estimates of $150,000, I want to say that it is not so. The difference is the diffex-enee between the estimate made in February last of the quantity of work that would likely be done within a given period and the quantity of work actually done. This is a difficult thing for an engineer to estimate. It depends upon the season and the contractor's ability and resources. In February last they thought they would require $450,000, and now we see that we only require $300,000, but the balance will come ia the future.

In reference to the statement the hon. Minister of Finance makes as to the difficulty in calculating the expenditure I would refer him to the example of the United States and Great Britain. There is, for instance, a public work that requires $10,000,000 to complete, and there is a vote of $1,500,000 to carry on the work for the year. Not one dollar is expended over the $1,500,000 that is voted by Congress or by the parliament of Great Britain for the purpose of doing the work. There are no supplementary estimates to supplement the votes granted by parliament for the purpose of carrying on an undertaking of that kind. Such a thing xiever occurs in Great Britain or in the United States, and there is no expenditure of a dollar beyond the amount that is voted by parliament or by Congress.
This money has not been paid. The work is going on and it is under conti-act.

The work is done and the certificates of the engineer who is in charge of the work are given to the contractor for the purpose of enabling him to collect his money. Suppose a contractor enters into a contract for doing a work that will cost $2,000,000, and $500,000 is voted for the work. The contractor expends $750,000, and he gets certificates from the engineer lTom day to day showing the amount of work done. The engineer of the department notifies the contractor when the $500,000 is expended that they will give him no more certificates and no more money until there is a further sum voted by parliament.
Mi-. BARKER, The hon. minister seems to think that because this woi-k in excess of the estimate of last year has been done it is not to be questioned. If the work has been done even without authority of parliament the country has to pay for it, and the objection that the bon. member for Lanai'k (Hon. Mr. Haggart) makes is that the department puts this country under an obligation to pay

a large sum of money beyond what parliament has authorized the department to contract for. We found a year ago that-in this same department $50,000 worth of work was done on one part of the canal system without one dollar having been authorized to be spent by parlament. What did the members of the government do when they came here last year ? They said that the country is in honour bound to pay for this work because it has been done.' Not only had parliament not authorized the work, it had refused to authorize it, yet $50,000 of an expenditure was incurred and we had last year to pass a special supplementary vote to pay for it. In precisely the same way last year we authorized a certain sum of money to be expended upon this railway work, and we are now asked to provide $300,000 more than parliament authorized.

This is a contract for a large and important work, and the contract has been before parliament and parliament has full knowledge of it, and we are voting from year to year as much money as will probably meet the requirements of the year in fulfilment of that contract. But if that is not enough, we are still bound ultimately to pay. There is a condition in all these contracts that payment will be made only when parliament has voted the money. These people have not received any money beyond the sum voted by parliament, and therefore the right of parliament to control the expenditure is preserved. Parliament approved of the contract and accepted the responsibility for providing all the money necessary for its fulfilment, and if it does-not provide it all in one year, it must in another. There is no violation of the principle of parliamentary control over the expenditure.

Does the minister mean to contend that because he inserts in a contract a provision that the money shall only be paid when parliament authorizes it, that he could in the face of this country say after the work ha'd been done that the contractors would not be paid ? Does not he know that when the government undertakes a work of that kind the country is as much bound in honour to pay for it as if parliament had authorized it ? In the work I referred to last year there was no pretense that parliament authorized it, and yet the minister asked that parliament should vote the $50,000, because we were in honour bound to do so. If you expend $300,000 more on this work, you bind this country to pay it just as much as if it had been passed in the estimates. What we are contending for is that the government is expected to so conduct the business that we shall not be put in the position that we are in honour bound to pay money that we have never authorized. When the minister says that it is impossible to define exactly what Mr. BARKER.
shall be expended upon a particular work, surely he does not mean to say that a department of the government may exceed its estimates by $300,000 on one item ? I could understand that in any business corporation the estimate might be exceeded by say $5,000 at most, but when it comes down to an excess of $300,000 in one year, it shows that the government, as now conducted, is absolutely reckless of what parliament authorized, and that it is simply going as it pleases.

The hon. gentleman is entirely wrong in assuming that there has been any excess of expenditure over and above (the estimate. This contract was laid before parliament and parliament has dealt with it, and thereby recognized its obligation, and the government is justified in going on and doing all the work contemplated by the contract.
Then why do you take any estimate for it each year ?

Because you cannot pay a dollar until i>arliament votes it. Suppose we enter into a contract for $1,000,000 for a work stretching over a number of years, and it turns out that in a given year, while you only estimate for $000,000, you need $700,000, would you stop the work ? No ; but you would tell the contractor that he could not get the balance of his money until parliament voted it, and if he sees fit to go on and do the work until parliament votes the money, it would be a legitimate transaction. The foundation of the whole thing is a contract that has been communicated to parliament and of which parliament has approved.
What was the amount voted last year for this item ?

air. BARKER. And you expended $800,000. Is that business ?
The ailNISTER OF FINANCE. Under a contract for a larger sum with which parliament was fully acquainted.

The ailNISTER OF FINANCE. That is the subject of an arrangement witl) the government of Prince Edward Island, and I will bring down the document.
air. aiONK. The minister has stated that the difficulties between the Grand Trunk Railway and the Intercolonial Railway have been submitted to arbitration.
It is agreed that they should be submitted to arbitration. The arbitration has not taken place.

Will the minister be good enough to bring down the correspondence relating to difficulties in regard to freight between the Grand Trunk Railway and the Intercolonial Railway, and the deed submitting that difficulty to arbitration ?
I will Inquire into the matter.
No doubt there is correspondence on the subject ?
I presume so, but I am not aware what it is.
If there is any, I suppose the minister will bring it down ?
I will look at it before I decide. I know of no objection.
Is there a lease of the waterpower on the Soulanges canal, and if so, is there only one lease ?
There is [DOT]one lease.
What is the amount payable by the lessee of that water-power ?
The deputy cannot give me the information now, but that also I will bring down.
Who is the contractor in charge of the lighting of the Cornwall *canal ?
Mr. M. P. Davis.
He is the lessee of the power ?
Yes.
For how many years has this contract been granted to Mr. Davis, and what is the annual amount payable by the government to him for the lighting of the canal ?

The contract is for twenty years ; but I would rather bring down the information after reference to the papers.
Soulanges canal-construction and equipment, $155,000.

This is made up of a variety of items : Extra motors and tools, $5,000 ; store-house and repair shops, $10,000, Canadian Genera) Electric Company, balance on contract, $6,000 ; labour for 1902-3, $2,000 ; lighting canal, 1902-3, $5,000 ; final estimates on sections one and two, $40,000 ; on sections four, five, six and seven, $30,000 ; on section thirteen, $26,000; probable payments
of additional items, $31,000; making the round sum of $155,000.
Has my hon. friend been informed that Mr. Davis has sold the right .which he secured from the government a year or two ago ?
The deputy informs me that we have no knowledge of that.
What is the present term of that lease ? Was it extended within the past, year or so ?
The lease was made a couple of years ago. It was not extended. The deputy is not quite sure of the length of time. That I will ascertain.

Have the contracts that were made been fulfilled ? We had a good deal of discussion about the advantages that Montreal would have from that concession. We were told that we would have lower rates. I would like to know how that matter stands now.
I am not able to give the hon. gentleman the information at present. I will ascertain it.
Is the statement the hon. minister has given a final estimate for the Soulanges canal ?
There is a sum of $10,000 which we ask for in the main estimates.
Is that the final estimate for the whole work ?
The deputy says unless there are some claims for extras, which he has not heard of, so far as he knows, this will cover everything.
What I want to know is whether the final estimates have been sent to the department for all the works on the Soulanges canal ?

The
final estimates are not in ; but we are making an allowance for balances due on the final estimates, so that the figures I have given are supposed to cover everything.
Surely the final estimates have been prepared for that work. Who is the engineer in charge of the work now ?
Mr. Alexander Grant. He succeeded Mr. Monro, who died.

speechtext: There was $100,000 voted for 1902-3 to carry on this work to the 1st of July, 1903.
This is for additional work.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The minister spent that $100,000 and $150,000 more ?
Yes, apparently.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And all the work under contract. How did his officers come to prepare estimates last year on which the minister asked parliament for $100,000 to carry on the work for the year, and he was $150,000 out ?
I cannot answer my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That $150,000 was spent without the authority of parliament. My hon. friend says that these estimates which we are now asked to vote were made up in February. The other estimates were only made up at the session preceding this one, and the money asked for was not enough by $150,000. Who has the contract for lighting the Soulanges canal ?
The government do that themselves.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What is the cost of lighting the Soulanges canal, which the government are doing as compared with the contract that has been let to Mr. Davis for lighting the Cornwall canal ?

I will endeavour to get the figures, if I can.
Trent canal-construction, $235,000.

This seems to be a similar case. We had an appropriation for the year of $300,000, but it appears that that appropriation was insufficient, and we require this sum to meet the following payments :	Peterborough-
Lakefield division, section 1, Corry & Laver-dulres, $89,100; lift-lock, Dominion Bridge Company, $55,000 ; Simcoe-Balsam division, section 1, A. Onderdonk, $5,000 ; section 2, Larkin & Sangster, $10,000 ; section 3, Brown & Aylmer, $18,600 ; bridges, Hamilton Bridge Company, $9,000 ; cement, A. T. Rowley, $11,300 ; land and damages, $11,300 ; Peterborough-Lakefield division, engineering and other expenses $5,000 ; Simcoe-Balsam division, $5,000 ; Simcoe-Georgian Bay division, $11,000 ; making a total of $235,000.

This expenditure has been going on for some twenty-two or twenty-three years and now sums up an enormous total. I am not objecting to that, but I think the country should know what return it is likely to get on this enormous expenditure on the Trent canal. That is one of those things which make it very desirable that the government should carry out the promise it made at the beginning of the session to appoint a transportation commission. The report of such a commission would probably contain the suggestion that our expenditure on that canal should be consider-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: ably curtailed. At any rate it is due to the country that the government should state to what extent it is going on with this work. Is it going to build a branch canal to Port Hope ? Is it going to extend the canals through to Georgian Bay ? And what is the estimate of the total cost when finished ?

I can give the amount expended in the past and the amount required to complete our outstanding contracts, but, I am not prepared to make any statement as to what may be done beyond that. Up to the 28th of February,. 1903, the expenditure was $3,907,577.

It is like crying over spilt milk to talk about what we have expended. What we are more anxious about is for the government to decide on a settled policy as to what it is going to do. Is it going on tn spend $20,000,000 or $30,000,000 without knowing where it is going to end V Has the government any plans as to future -work on this canal 1 Have surveys been made ?

I am not able to give my hon. friend any information which has not been already given. Certain sections are under contract and these have to be completed. I can give information of what they have cost and what it will cost to finish them.
And then ?
That is another story.

It is ' the then ' which I am trying to get at. The government put the promise into His Excellency's mouth that we would have a transportation commission. This is one of the questions which would come before that commission. In the future before a work of that kind is begun, we should have some little knowledge of where it is going to end. This has been going on, under all governments, for some twenty years. I have been finding fault occasionally with works done in other provinces of the Dominion and asking what revenues are derived from them. If you are getting an adequate revenue, there is no need to find fault, but this work is not likely ever to pay one per cent on the cost of its construction, and probably will never pay running expenses. It is high time therefore to call a halt. This vote is a good text for a sermon and now is a good time to deliver it. I cannot be found fault with on the ground that I only oppose expenditure when it is to be made in some of the other provinces and do not oppose it nearer home. This is a case near home. The country through which this canal is passing is one of the most magnificent in the world. The people there want a waterway through their counties and townships, especially about election time. But it seems to me that the government should be strong enough and able enough-especially a government about

*whose strong and bold policy in connection with another large work we hear so much about-to decide on a policy with regard to this work. It is not an insignificant work. It has already cost $4,000,000 and will cost another $4,000,000 before it is finished, and then it will not be a ship canal, but only a canal for tow-boats.
Twenty thousand bushel tow-boats.
The same depth as the Erie canal now.

If we want to compare it with the Erie canal, we should spend $110,000,000 on it. We should tear it up and build a new one as they are doing with the Erie canal. Those who started the work had good intentions, but things have changed since. A canal drawing four or five of water might answer in those days ; but with the larger ideas of the present day, this matter should be reconsidered before we spend any more money. At any rate the government should come down with a complete scheme, showing whether they propose to build it to the Georgian bay and what it will cost.

I am surprised at the lack of breadth displayed by the hon. gentleman. I have always admired him when he urged the people of Canada to tax themselves some for the benefit of the woollen trade and the labouring people engaged in that industry. I have voted for that encouragement, and I cannot conceive how a man can be so broad on one subject and so contracted on another. There is a report on this canal prepared, after years of consideration, by the most eminent men who could be obtained at the time. Mr. Kennedy, of Montreal, was one, Mr. Turner, of Toronto, was another, and the name of the third, I forget ; but their report has been on the Table for years, and it amply justifies the expenditure we have made. All I have to say to my hon. friend is that if he will take a holiday and spend a few days with me on a trip over the route of that canal, I will convince him that it is a work of the greatest importance to the Dominion. I am sorry to say that men who ought to be prepared to take a broader national view of this question stand in their places and belittle a great work like this, because it does not happen to touch the one-horse city of Toronto. I would ask the hon. minister to give me the items of expenditure that have taken place.
I have already read the list, which the hon. gentleman will find in ' Hansard.'
Is no more to be expended here than this sum ?
This is for the past year. There is also a sum in the main estimates for the current year.
Is the lift-lock at Peterborough completed ?
No, I am advised that it will be ready in a month or so.

I think the House is entitled to know the government's policy with regard to this matter. If we are to go on with the work it is better to go on with it now. I do not share the view expressed by the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock). Even if the Trent Valley canal is not destined to be a through route it will be an accommodation to the farming community and the industrial community in that part of the country. I happen to have travelled over the Trent Valley canal system. It is true that it goes through one of the most fertile parts of the country. Already the farming community rely a great deal upon that work, and, if I am not mistaken, there is a pretty large freight traffic there. Recently, for instance, there has been a very large industry established at Peterborough for the manufacture of cereal foods. They expect to use about a million bushels of grain a year, and they expect that grain, or most of it, to reach them through the Trent Valley system.
It comes in farmers' sleighs and wagons.

My information comes from the promoters of the scheme themselves. In any event, I think the House is entitled to know what the hon. gentlemen on the Treasury benches intend to do. The Trent Valley canal system has already cost $4,000,000, and I think the Department of Railways and Canals has an estimate before it showing that it will cost $4,000,000 to complete it. Rightly or wrongly, the country has invested $4,000,000 in this work. It would be a great pity, after having spent so much money, not to complete the work. In any case, it will be a useful work. It is true it is not a deep <|anal, but then the Erie canal is not a deep canal, yet it has served a very good purpose indeed. And if I remember well, it would not involve a great additional expenditure to get another two feet of depth throughout this system. This would give eight feet of water. Well, that is a pretty good canal. It will afford, a through route between Georgian bay and Lake Ontario. I make the prophecy that barges of small size will carry large quantities of grain and general freight on that canal. It would be a pity to waste the money we have already spent, and it would be to a certain extent wasted money if the work were not completed. After having gone over the succession of lakes that form part of the system, I have come to the conclusion that the completion of the work is a question worthy of our most serious consideration.

As to the policy in connection with this canal there are, as the hon. member (Hon. Mr. Tarte) suggested, two aspects of the case-the local and the general or national. Of the two the national is more important and the one more likely to be important in the future. Undoubtedly it will be a work of great local benefit. But as soon as the works are completed at Peterborough and between Lake Simcoe and Balsam lake, there will be a complete chain of navigation from Washago, at the head of Lake Couchiching, to Camp-[DOT]bellford. And when the extensions at either end are finished there will be navigation between Midland on Georgian bay and the Bay of Quint6 at Trenton-or, my hon. friend from East Durham (Mr. Ward) will claim, at Port Hope. And 1 have no fear whatever of any government having the hardihood to resist the demand for completion of the work once these two links now under construction are completed, because the advantage of the work will be so clear that even our friend the acting Minister of Railways and Canals will be only too pleased to propose the necessary votes to finish the work. I have no fear of the future policy. As to the utility of the canal or its carrying capacity, that is ancient history. The ai'guments have been gone over and are well known. There may be some few members who, for reasons of their own will not learn, like the former member for North Wellington. But I shall not insult the intelligence of the House by repeating the arguments that already appear in ' Hansard ' of other sessions explaining the utility of this work.

I do not wish to prolong the discussion. But I would merely point out. that the strongest argument made use of in favour of the completion of this work is that we have already spent a large amount of money, and, in order to get back something of what we have spent, it will be necessary to spend more. It will be a very expensive business to provide a,depth of eight feet in this canal. It will very nearly double the expense of construction, because the whole canal will have to be widened in order to make it deeper. I still maintain the ground I took that, in entering upon a work of this kind, we should count the cost. I believe that if the proposal now came first before parliament to expend the money we have spent, $4,000,000, to build what we have already completed, this House would kick it out unceremoniously. We would not think of it five minutes. Not a man would favour it. The Minister of Finance would be one of the first to cry out against such an expenditure for this purpose. However, the government has spent this money and they will go on spending. There are votes in it.

I regret that my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) displays such utter ignorance with regard to canals. He says it would be necessary to widen the canal in order to deepen it. It is already 32 feet wide.
Either it is too wide now, or you would have to widen it in order to deepen it.

The canal is at present 32 feet wide and the locks are 132' feet long, with 6 feet of water on the sills. Land has already been purchased to deepen the canal to 8 feet. The people of this country knew what they were doing when they voted this money ; this estimate has been before the House. I regret that some people unfortunately listened to the objections of the gentlemen who formerly composed the opposition, and some members of the Liberal-Conservative party became imbued with the narrow teachings of those gentlemen. I am sorry that my hon. friend displayed such a lack of knowledge concerning this canal. It is already 32 feet wide, the land is already purchased for deepening it to 8 feet whenever it is necessary. There is only one drawback, in my opinion, and it is formed on the opinion of competent engineers, it would have been better had the locks been mor-e than 132 feet long. But it is not an ordinary canal, being a continuation of a series of lakes, and as the tugs would readily tow a large number of these boats, it does not matter much about the len'gth, seeing that it has such a good breadth. Barges could be constructed to carry 50,000 bushels of grain, so that four or five of them would take the grain from the largest vessels that enters the harbours along our great lakes.
Under the terms of the contract, when is it required to be finished between Lake Simcoe and Balsam lake ?
At the end of the present season, with the exception of the lift-lock.
Is there a contract now existing for placing the lift-lock at Kirk-field ?
No.
How far is that work advanced for placing the piers for a lift-lock at Kirkfield ?
The concrete work is advancing rapidly. The lift-lock at Peterborough will be. open probably in a month or six weeks.
It is a very fine piece of work.

When that is completed the water can be let in the canal from Kirkfield, which is within about 12 miles of

Lake Simcoe, and there will be uninterrupted water communication to within about 10 miles of Lake Ontario.
Within 15 miles of Lake Ontario.
How much will that lift lock cost, with the extras, &c. ?
I will have to bring that down on another occasion.
Last year we had some information with reference to a contract on this canal taken by Corry & Laver -dure. Did that go to the Exchequer Court for settlement ?
It was referred to three engineers.
What was their verdict ?
The report was favourable to the contractors.
How much has been awarded to them ?

I want to know what the award was, and what is the difference between the award and the report of the engineer of the department ? I would like to know why the dispute did not go to the Exchequer Court, which was established for that purpose ?
I will bring down the information.

There was a vote of $300,000 for this last year. I am not finding fault with the expenditure of a large sum of money for what I call a very laudable work. But there has been $235,000 over-expended on a vote of $300,000 last year.

I think I ought to say a word generally for the officials of the department in this matter. Very often the Finance Minister and his colleagues in the government object to giving these departments all the money they ask for. It is not an uncommon thing, where the engineers report they would like a large amount of money, for us to reach a conclusion that may be they will not need it all before the end of the year, and we try to cut them down, and sometimes we cut them down severely. I am not prepared to say that is the case with this particular item. But I am afraid that I am myself at times to blame for cutting down where I think the demands are too large, and perhaps at times the reports of the engineers would warrant a larger appropriation than we are willing to give ihem.

The explanation of the Finance Minister raises the very point that I have been discussing this session and the last two sessions. He tells us .that the officers of the department often ask for more money than the ministers are willing to grant them. Now, that might be well enough. The ministers are responsible for the expenditure. They come down to parliament and say what they want parliament to grant them. They cut down their officers' estimates, and if they do that upon their responsibility and get parliament to vote the money, well and good. But do they rest there ? Not at all. They come here and ask us to vote less than they know their officers require, and after getting parliament to vote the lesser amount, they go ahead and expend all the officers wanted.

The position taken by my hon. friend seems to be that the Minister of Finance and the other ministers should collectively give every individual minister all the public money he asks for. - I am afraid that is his conclusion. Still, we find the bon. gentleman condemning us for occasionally trying to keep the expenditure down. He will say that the minister should not expend more money than parliament votes. That may happen in some cases, but he ought to take into account the number of cases where they do not expend all the money voted because the appropriations have been cut down.

If the Finance Minister, when he is asking us for an estimate, would tell the House that the officers of the department asked, for instance, for $500,000, but that he thinks only* $300,000 should be expended, the House could then judge for themselves. The House may well say what
/

any business man would say, that we will not grant you $300,000 when you know it will be necessary to expend $500,000. We are entitled to know the facts, but bon. gentlemen conceal from this House the fact that their officers have told them that large sums of money were required for that work when they applied to this parliament to give them a grant, knowing that that sum would not do the work. Yet we find item after item throughout the whole of the estimates where hon. gentlemen are, after cutting down their officers' estimates by $50,000 or $60,000, going on and expending money that parliament has never been asked to authorize.
I would like to ask the hon. minister whether Corry & Laver-dure have received the amount of their award ?
I am advised that they have received part of it.
Is not a portion of this item to pay an amount that is still due to them ?
That is going to be taken out of this item ?

Yes.
lion. Mr. HAGGART. Is that part of the item that we are voting now ?
Has the hon. minister the award ?
No, but I will be glad to bring the information down.
Was the award approved by council ?
My recollection is that it was ultimately approved by council, but I would not like to speak positively on that point.
The hon. minister would not come down and ask for a vote unless with the approval of council.
Certainly not. My impression is that it was approved by council.
It was approved by council.
Can the hon. minister conveniently give the cost of the Grand Trunk bridge across the Trent valley canal near Gamebridge ?
I will have a note taken of the question, and bring the information down.

I would like to know from the hon. minister, if he bas not information in' his hands at the present moment, what reaeons were assigned in the Order in Council for taking this matter away from the Exchequer Court which was formed for the purpose of trying these cases ? Every contractor under the government has as much right to have his claim against the government dealt with in a special way as have these parties.

I will at a later stage bring down the information.
Sault. Ste.Marie canal-construction and equipment. $18,000.
What is ibis for ?'
This is to make further payment on account of the widening and deepening of the upper entrance, and extending the guide piers. By extending the guide piers the cross currents will be avoided.
What will be required to complete that work ?
There is $94,000 in the main estimates for the current year which will probably finish it.
Will that give a 20-foot navigation both coming into the canal and going out of it ?
Yes, 20 feet, 5 inches.
Is any effort being made to build a wharf on the Canadian side ? It seems very strange to see our boats calling at the American side to land their cargoes.

Not only should we build a wharf there, buti we should carry out dredging work on a pretty large scale. When I left office I had contemplated going on with that work, but nothing has been done since. It is a very great pity indeed. I can only repeat what I said last year, that it is a shame to this country that even government boats cannot take coal at a Canadian wharf. There' is not enough water, but I am very much afraid that party politics has a good deal to do with the delay. It is a great pity.
Is there any government wharf nearby the canal ?

Yes, but tbere is not enough wrater. There should be another wharf built, there should be dredging done, and there should be spent at that point to carry out the work that should be carried out over a quarter of million dollars. It is not a large sum of money for such neces-

sary work there. This is a very important point. We are losing a vast quantity of trade by not carrying out that work.

There is another point in connection with the matter to which I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Finance. I have asked the officers wiiy boats do not go through the Canadian canal. Among other reasons which they assign why vessels choose the American side is that they take coal on the American side, and in that way save the duty. If these steamers are going up and down these waters using coal on the upper lakes, and if, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte), we are losing a great deal of trade by reason of the boats passing through the Yankee canal, could we not arrange for them to get their coal duty free ?
Free trade ?

If steamers, by going to the American side can get their coal to be used on the open lakes free of duty, why cannot an arrangement be made by which they could have the same advantage on the Canadian side ?

They can get their coal free of duty on the Canadian side. If vessels navigating the great lakes take a supply of coal on the Canadian side, they get it free of duty at Port Colborne, Sault Ste. Marie, or at any other point on the great lakes. I quite agree with the hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's, that the government should expend a large amount of money at Sault Ste. Marie on the water front. There Is no dock at the Soo, at which the upper lake boats can land. The Canadian Pacific Railway boats invariably go through the American canal, mainly, i believe, because the channel into the Canadian canal is not a proper and sufficient channel. In the first place it is a crooked channel. They have to make a detour of a very considerable extent to get into the mouth of the Canadian canal. It is only being excavated now by blasting-rock and taking it out in dredges. I think the government should spend a very considerable sum of money in making our Canadian canal and what you might call the harbour at Sault Ste. Marie suitable for the upper lake traffic. If that were done, our Canadian boats would more largely use the Canadian canal than at present.

As this is one of the great highways of commerce along which thousands and thousands of people travel passing from the east to the west, and from the west to the east, on their way around the world, when these people find that our own boats do not call at the Canadian side, it seems to me that it is humiliating to a nation like Canada. We have boats doing
an immense trade, and when we go on these boats we are landed on the American side and have to cross over to the Canadian side on a ferry which is scarcely large enough to cross the Ottawa river.
Is it only the question of a wharf ?

We want a better wharf and a greater depth of water. I am told that they have the advantage, in calling at the American side, of coaling up. Why should they not call at the Canadian side and then call at the American side if necessary to coal up ? It only requires a little additional time to call at the Canadian side. They always have trade for the American side, let them call there and coal up, if the customs regulations are such that they cannot get their coal free of duty unless they call at the American side. It is humiliating to hear Americans remarking on the manner in which the Canadian canal is kept Surely from year to year this should not be allowed to go on without an effort to remedy it. It is a bad advertisement for Canada, and it is not in keeping with what you would, expect from a progressive government.

The real fact is that we have neglected our waterways for a great many years. Some of us have vainly tried to convince the House and the country of the necessity of improving our waterways. But while a vote of $50,000,000 for railways does not frighten us, yet when public men who have studied the question carefully come before parliament with data to prove that the waterways are the only means of keeping our trade, we are called down every time. Plow many times has it not happened to me that I have asked $50,000 for a work that should have been done, but I could not get it ; not because my colleagues were ill-disposed but because public opinion was not wideawake. The Americans are spending millions to deepen the St. Mary's river. They have the trade today on the lakes because they have equipped their harbours and deepened their rivers while we have done scarcely anything. Our harbours are shallow and we do not seem to be disposed to go on with the work of improvement which is necessary. The work at Sault Ste. Marie should be done and a great many other works on our rivers and harbours should be done also. I apprehend that the supplementary estimates this year will not bring us much relief on that account, because I see with sorrow and regret that there does not seem to be a disposition to give our water ways that consideration which they deserve. When you build railways you will be still confronted with the waterways of the Americans. The trade is going through these channels now. You will build railways, and the American waterways will

take the trade from you all the same, unless you make your own waterways able to compete with theirs.

The hon. member (Mr. German) has read a statement that the coal supplied by these vessels on the Canadian side is free of duty. Will the Minister of Customs give us an official statement on the subject.
Coal to taken out of store for vessels that are navigated on the lakes is free, the same as other ships' stores.

Suppose a vessel starts from Owen Sound to Port Arthur, it has to pay duty on the coal it takes at Owen Sound and the consequence is that the vessel takes a cargo of coal at Sault Ste. Marie to carry it to Owen Sound and back again. It is true it gets it free when in transit, but at the starting point our vessels are handicapped.

Is it not correct that a boat leaving Owen Sound takes coal upon which duty has been paid and as she requires more coal when she gets to the ' Soo,' she goes through the American lock and gets American coal free of duty ? I understand there was a regulation at one time by which when vessels were towing logs to the other side they were permitted to bring in coal in bond, but where a vessel takes coal at a Canadian port, duty has been paid on that coal.

In view of what the hon. gentleman says I would not speak positively, but I will refresh my memory as to what the regulations are. You say that a boat loading at Owen Sound and going across the Georgian bay to another of our ports-
Going to the ' Soo ' and up to Port William.
That she has to pay duty at Owen Sound, and she brings enough to take her back ?

No, but the coal she takes on at Owen Sound has paid the duty, and then wheii she needs a fresh supply at Sault Ste. Marie she goes to the American side to take coal on, upon which there is no duty1 payable. If she went through the Canadian lock at the ' Soo ' she would have to take coal that had paid duty.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman whether it Is not a fact that at Owen Sound the coal merchants have bonded warehousesi so that a steamer taking coal on board there would take it out of bond ?

The general principle covering the matter is that ships' stores are free. How it would affect a particular ship sailing to particular ports, Hon. Mr. TAR.TE.
I do not know. Stores may be taken- out of the bonded warehouse free of duty.

My object was to impress upon the Minister of Customs the point brought out by the member for Fron-tenae (Mr. Calvin) that there might be some arangement made whereby the coal could be stored on the Canadian side and if it were used for this purpose, duty would not be paid on it. I think the hon. member for Frontenac is wrong when he says that the coal can be taken out of bond. That would hardly be the case unless the object was to encourage the vessels to trade with our own Canadian ports.
Ships' stores come out of bond without, paying duty.
Coal is not ships' stores, and it is used in trading from Canadian ports and not to foreign ports.

I can speak from absolute experience on the matter in so far as vessels ' in transitu ' are concerned. I do not know what' it would be starting from Owen Sound, but I know that vessels passing through the Welland canal and through the Sault canal can take on coal at Port Colborne and at the Canadian Sault without paying duty.

There is no doubt that after building the canal at the Sault, we have neglected to add wharfs and other necessary accomodation. I think it is humiliating for any of us who go up on the boats to find them on all occasions passing through the American canal. I have gone up many times, and on no occasion, either going or coming, has the vessel passed through our own canal. I understood that one of the reasons was that the coal was dutiable when taken on at the Canadian Sault ; but the main reason undoubtedly is that there is no wharf accommodation, and that the approaches to the canal on both sides are quite inadequate for large boats to pass through the Canadian canal. In connection with that, I may say that if any of us would take a map showing the lighthouses on the Georgian bay and on our part of the shore with the numerous lighthouses dotted everywhere on the American side, we must be struck with the feeling either that we have no business on our side of the lakes or that we have entirely neglected our waters. It is very startling to see how few lighthouses we have on our side and how completely the Americans have lighted their channels and how easy they have made the approaches to their canals. I understood the hon. member for St. Mary's to say that he thought we were not spending money because it was a party question. I do not think there would be any objection on this side, of the House to having a very liberal expenditure on our waterways, especially

on this key to our great waterway from Lake Superior down to our ports on the Georgian bay. I believe that both sides of the House would endorse making the channel thoroughly easy for Canadian boats.
Parran's Point Canal, enlargement, $7,000.

This is to pay a balance due to the 30th June, 1903, for work done by the Canadian Construction Company under contract. There is a further sum of $12,000 for this work in the main estimates, and these two sums will practically complete the entire work. The canal is now open.	,

The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.
What will be the order of business for to-morrow ?

It may be that some of the Bills on the Order paper will be proceeded with. I am not quite sure of that; but we will probably take Supply. The Minister of Trade and Ct mmerce will take his estimates, and then we will pass on to railvi ays.
